title: Prompt CI, Canary/Shadow, Rollbacks, Vendor Abstraction & Forecasting
scopeHtml: Scope: Release engineering for GenAI: prompt CI, safe rollouts, multi-layer rollback, version compatibility, vendor abstraction and cost/capacity forecasting.

notes.title: Why GenAI releases need their own discipline
notes.html:
In normal backend work, a release is a new build of code. You run unit tests, deploy, watch error rates, and roll back if they go up. The behaviour of the code is deterministic: same input, same output.

A GenAI feature is different in four ways:

  1. The behaviour lives in text, not code. A prompt (the instructions you send to the model) is a string. Changing one sentence can change the answers for thousands of inputs. There is no compiler to tell you something broke.
  2. The model is not yours. With a hosted API (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google), the provider can retire a model id, change safety filters, or silently update a "latest" alias. Your code did not change, but your product did.
  3. The output is probabilistic. The same input can give different outputs (controlled by temperature, a setting where 0 means "pick the most likely word each time" and higher means more random). A test that passes once might fail the next run.
  4. Failures are quiet. A broken prompt rarely throws an exception. It returns a fluent, confident, wrong answer with HTTP 200. Your dashboards stay green while users get worse answers.

So the release process has to add things classic CI/CD does not have: quality evaluations as a gate, gradual exposure (canary and shadow), rollback across several layers (prompt, model, embeddings, index, config), compatibility tracking between those layers, an abstraction against vendors, and forecasting because cost scales with tokens, not with servers.

Classic release:      code ---> unit tests ---> deploy ---> watch errors/latency
GenAI release:  code + prompt + model + embeddings + index + config
                  |
                  v
          prompt CI (evals) ---> shadow ---> canary ---> full rollout
                  ^                                          |
                  +----------- multi-layer rollback <--------+

Real-life analogy (after the explanation): shipping a prompt change without these steps is like a restaurant changing its recipe and serving it to every table at once without tasting it. Prompt CI is the kitchen taste test, shadow is cooking the new dish for staff only, canary is offering it to two tables, and rollback is being able to put the old recipe card back.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "we have unit tests" as the answer. A unit test on a prompt string proves nothing about model behaviour; you need evals that actually call the model.
  • Treating green HTTP metrics as proof of health. GenAI failures are semantic, so you must monitor quality signals too.
  • Forgetting that the provider is part of your release surface: model aliases and deprecations change behaviour without a deploy of yours.

notes.title: Prompt CI: the pipeline
notes.html:
What it is. Prompt CI (continuous integration for prompts) means: every time someone changes a prompt, a model id, a retrieval setting or a tool definition, an automated job runs a fixed set of test cases through the real system and blocks the merge if quality drops.

Why it exists. Prompts are edited by many people (developers, product managers, domain experts) and each edit "looks fine" when you try three examples by hand. Hand testing hides regressions: fixing the case you looked at silently breaks ten you did not.

How it works, step by step.

  1. Keep prompts as files in git (for example prompts/support_answer.v7.txt), not strings buried in code or a database someone can edit without review.
  2. Keep a golden set: a versioned file of test cases. Each case has an input, plus either an expected answer, a list of facts that must appear, a rule that must hold (for example "never mention competitor names"), or a rubric for a judge.
  3. On every pull request that touches prompts, models or retrieval config, CI runs all cases against the candidate and (cached) against the baseline (the version currently in production).
  4. Each output is scored. Three scorer types, from cheapest to most expensive:
    • Deterministic checks: JSON parses, schema is valid, required keyword present, length under limit, no banned phrase, a tool was called with the right arguments. Free and stable.
    • Reference-based metrics: exact match, similarity to an expected answer using embeddings.
    • LLM-as-judge: another model grades the output with a rubric (for example "is every claim supported by the provided context? Answer PASS or FAIL"). Flexible but itself noisy and costs tokens.
  5. CI computes aggregate scores per category (accuracy, safety, format, tone) and compares them with the baseline.
  6. If any gate fails, the PR cannot merge. The report shows which cases regressed so a human can read the actual outputs.
PR changes prompts/support_answer.txt
        |
        v
  load golden set (400 cases, tagged by category)
        |
        +--> run candidate (N=3 samples per case) --> score
        +--> load cached baseline scores
        |
        v
  compare per category:  schema 100%?  safety 100%?  quality >= baseline - 1pt?
        |
   pass / fail --> PR status + report with the regressed cases

The core of a runner in Python. It calls the model, applies a deterministic check, and returns a pass rate:

import json, os
import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()  # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from the environment

def run_case(system_prompt: str, user_input: str) -> str:
    msg = client.messages.create(
        model=os.getenv("CANDIDATE_MODEL", "claude-sonnet-5-5"),
        max_tokens=500,
        temperature=0,
        system=system_prompt,
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": user_input}],
    )
    return msg.content[0].text

def check(case: dict, output: str) -> bool:
    try:
        data = json.loads(output)            # deterministic gate 1: valid JSON
    except json.JSONDecodeError:
        return False
    return all(k in data for k in case["required_keys"])  # gate 2: schema keys

def pass_rate(prompt_path: str, golden_path: str) -> float:
    prompt = open(prompt_path, encoding="utf8").read()
    cases = [json.loads(line) for line in open(golden_path, encoding="utf8")]
    ok = sum(check(c, run_case(prompt, c["input"])) for c in cases)
    return ok / len(cases)   # prints e.g. 0.97 meaning 97% of cases passed

if __name__ == "__main__":
    rate = pass_rate("prompts/support_answer.txt", "golden/support.jsonl")
    print(f"pass rate {rate:.3f}")
    raise SystemExit(0 if rate >= 0.95 else 1)   # non-zero exit fails the CI job

The same idea in Kotlin, against your own backend endpoint (so the runner tests the real code path, including retrieval and post-processing). It uses the JDK HTTP client and assumes the golden file is a list of input strings:

import java.net.URI
import java.net.http.HttpClient
import java.net.http.HttpRequest
import java.net.http.HttpResponse
import java.io.File

val http: HttpClient = HttpClient.newHttpClient()

fun ask(baseUrl: String, input: String): String {
    val body = """{"question": ${quote(input)}}"""
    val req = HttpRequest.newBuilder(URI.create("$baseUrl/answer"))
        .header("Content-Type", "application/json")
        .POST(HttpRequest.BodyPublishers.ofString(body))
        .build()
    return http.send(req, HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString()).body()
}

fun quote(s: String) = "\"" + s.replace("\\", "\\\\").replace("\"", "\\\"") + "\""

fun main() {
    val inputs = File("golden/support_inputs.txt").readLines()
    // Cheap deterministic check: the response must be non-empty and contain the "answer" key.
    val passed = inputs.count { val r = ask("http://localhost:8080", it); r.contains("\"answer\"") }
    val rate = passed.toDouble() / inputs.size
    println("pass rate %.3f".format(rate))          // e.g. pass rate 0.970
    if (rate < 0.95) kotlin.system.exitProcess(1)   // fail the CI job
}

And Java (same endpoint, same gate):

import java.net.URI;
import java.net.http.*;
import java.nio.file.*;
import java.util.List;

public class PromptCi {
    static final HttpClient HTTP = HttpClient.newHttpClient();

    static String ask(String baseUrl, String input) throws Exception {
        String body = "{\"question\": \"" + input.replace("\\", "\\\\").replace("\"", "\\\"") + "\"}";
        HttpRequest req = HttpRequest.newBuilder(URI.create(baseUrl + "/answer"))
            .header("Content-Type", "application/json")
            .POST(HttpRequest.BodyPublishers.ofString(body))
            .build();
        return HTTP.send(req, HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString()).body();
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        List<String> inputs = Files.readAllLines(Path.of("golden/support_inputs.txt"));
        int passed = 0;
        for (String in : inputs) {
            if (ask("http://localhost:8080", in).contains("\"answer\"")) passed++;
        }
        double rate = (double) passed / inputs.size();
        System.out.printf("pass rate %.3f%n", rate);   // e.g. pass rate 0.970
        if (rate < 0.95) System.exit(1);               // fail the CI job
    }
}

Real tools. Open-source and commercial eval runners that fit in CI include promptfoo (YAML test cases, runs from the command line), OpenAI Evals, Ragas (RAG-focused metrics), DeepEval, LangSmith and Braintrust (hosted dataset and experiment tracking). Check each project's docs for current features (verify).

Everyday analogy. Prompt CI is the automated test suite a bakery would run on every new recipe: bake 400 test loaves, weigh them, taste a sample, and refuse to put the recipe in the book if too many come out flat.

Common interview traps.

  • "Set temperature to 0 and the test is deterministic." Not guaranteed: hosted models can still vary run to run (batching and hardware effects), and some models restrict sampling parameters. Plan for noise.
  • Testing only the model call. The regression may come from retrieval, chunking or post-processing, so test the real pipeline end to end.
  • Putting the golden set in the same PR as the prompt change with no review: authors can quietly weaken the tests.

notes.title: Prompt CI: gates, flakiness and cost
notes.html:
A pipeline that is flaky or too expensive gets ignored, so the engineering details matter.

Flakiness and sample size. If a case passes 90% of the time at your settings, a single run will randomly fail it one time in ten. Two fixes:

  • Run each case several times (N=3 to 5) and score the pass fraction, not a single boolean.
  • Compare the candidate with the baseline using a tolerance band, not an exact threshold. For example: "quality may not drop more than 1 point below the baseline, and the safety category must stay at 100%".

A rough rule for how many test cases you need: to detect a drop of d in a pass rate around p with decent confidence (about 80% power, 5% significance), you need roughly n = 16 * p * (1 - p) / d^2 cases per arm. Worked example: p = 0.90, d = 0.05, so n = 16 * 0.9 * 0.1 / 0.0025 = 1.44 / 0.0025 = 576. With 100 cases you can only reliably see big drops (about 12 points). That is a rule of thumb; it is why golden sets of 30 cases give false confidence.

Tiered gates. Run the cheap checks first and stop early:

Tier 0 (seconds, free)   lint prompt file: placeholders present, no secrets, size under limit
Tier 1 (1-2 min)         smoke set: 30 cases, deterministic checks only, every PR
Tier 2 (10-20 min)       full golden set + LLM judge, only when prompt/model/retrieval files changed
Tier 3 (nightly)         large regression set + adversarial/safety set + drift check on the pinned model

Cost of CI. Do the arithmetic before you build it. Suppose 400 cases, 3 samples each, 1,500 input tokens and 300 output tokens per call, plus a judge call of 2,000 input and 50 output tokens. Using illustrative prices of 3 dollars per million input tokens and 15 per million output tokens (verify current prices):

  • Candidate calls: 400 * 3 = 1,200 calls. Input 1,200 * 1,500 = 1.8M tokens = 1.8 * 3 = 5.40 dollars. Output 1,200 * 300 = 0.36M tokens = 0.36 * 15 = 5.40 dollars. Subtotal 10.80 dollars.
  • Judge calls: 1,200. Input 1,200 * 2,000 = 2.4M tokens = 7.20 dollars. Output 1,200 * 50 = 0.06M = 0.90 dollars. Subtotal 8.10 dollars.
  • Total about 18.90 dollars per full run. At 20 full runs a week that is about 378 dollars a week. Cache the baseline results (keyed by prompt hash + model + case id) so you only pay for the candidate, and use a cheaper model for the judge only after checking its agreement with a stronger judge on a labelled sample.

Judge hygiene. An LLM judge has biases: it prefers longer answers, prefers its own style, and can be sensitive to the order of two options. Mitigate by using a binary rubric per criterion, randomising order in pairwise comparisons, and periodically comparing the judge with human labels (track agreement).

A Python cache wrapper that makes the baseline free after the first run:

import hashlib, json, pathlib

CACHE = pathlib.Path(".eval_cache")
CACHE.mkdir(exist_ok=True)

def cache_key(prompt: str, model: str, case_id: str, sample: int) -> str:
    raw = f"{prompt}|{model}|{case_id}|{sample}".encode()
    return hashlib.sha256(raw).hexdigest()

def cached_run(prompt, model, case, sample, run_fn):
    f = CACHE / f"{cache_key(prompt, model, case['id'], sample)}.json"
    if f.exists():
        return json.loads(f.read_text())["output"]   # no API call, no cost
    out = run_fn(prompt, case["input"])
    f.write_text(json.dumps({"output": out}))
    return out

Kotlin version of the key function (the file cache logic is the same pattern):

import java.security.MessageDigest

fun cacheKey(prompt: String, model: String, caseId: String, sample: Int): String {
    val raw = "$prompt|$model|$caseId|$sample".toByteArray()
    return MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-256").digest(raw)
        .joinToString("") { "%02x".format(it) }   // 64-char hex string
}

Java version:

import java.security.MessageDigest;

static String cacheKey(String prompt, String model, String caseId, int sample) throws Exception {
    byte[] raw = (prompt + "|" + model + "|" + caseId + "|" + sample).getBytes();
    byte[] hash = MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-256").digest(raw);
    StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
    for (byte b : hash) sb.append(String.format("%02x", b));
    return sb.toString();   // 64-char hex string
}

Failure patterns.

  • The golden set was written from the old prompt's outputs, so it rewards the old style and blocks real improvements.
  • The set never changes, so the team overfits to it (the score is 99% and production complaints keep rising). Refresh it monthly with real failed production traces.
  • CI uses a different model alias than production, so it passes and production regresses.

Common interview traps.

  • "Our eval score went up, so the prompt is better." Only if the set is large, representative and the judge is validated.
  • Blocking on a single noisy judge score instead of a tolerance band plus hard gates on deterministic checks.
  • Forgetting to pin the exact model version in CI; a moving alias makes results non-reproducible.

notes.title: Shadow deployments
notes.html:
What it is. In a shadow deployment the new version receives a copy of real production traffic, produces answers, and those answers are never shown to users. You only record and compare them.

Why it exists. Golden sets are written by you; real users ask things you did not imagine. Shadow lets you see how the new prompt or model behaves on the real input distribution with zero user risk. It is the only safe way to find out the new version's real latency, token usage (cost) and failure rate before anyone is exposed.

How it works, step by step.

  1. The request arrives. The live (champion) pipeline handles it and returns the answer to the user as usual.
  2. Asynchronously (after or alongside the response, never blocking it), the request is copied to the shadow (challenger) pipeline.
  3. The challenger result is stored with the champion result and the request id.
  4. An offline job compares them: format validity, token counts, latency, refusal rate, and an LLM-judge or pairwise comparison on a sample.
  5. The team reads the cases where they disagree most, then decides to move to canary or fix the candidate.
user --> gateway --> champion --> response to user
            |
            +--(async copy, sampled 10%)--> challenger --> stored only
                                                |
                       offline compare (judge, schema, cost, latency)

Python: fire-and-forget shadow call that cannot hurt the user path:

import asyncio, random

SHADOW_RATE = 0.10

async def handle(request, champion, challenger, store):
    answer = await champion(request)                      # user waits only for this
    if random.random() < SHADOW_RATE:
        asyncio.create_task(shadow(request, answer, challenger, store))
    return answer

async def shadow(request, champion_answer, challenger, store):
    try:
        out = await asyncio.wait_for(challenger(request), timeout=30)
        await store.save(request.id, champion_answer, out)
    except Exception as e:          # shadow errors are data, never user-visible
        await store.save_error(request.id, repr(e))

Kotlin coroutines:

import kotlinx.coroutines.*
import kotlin.random.Random

val shadowScope = CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + Dispatchers.IO)

suspend fun handle(req: Request, champion: suspend (Request) -> String,
                   challenger: suspend (Request) -> String, store: Store): String {
    val answer = champion(req)                      // user path
    if (Random.nextDouble() < 0.10) {
        shadowScope.launch {                        // separate scope: failures stay isolated
            runCatching { withTimeout(30_000) { challenger(req) } }
                .onSuccess { store.save(req.id, answer, it) }
                .onFailure { store.saveError(req.id, it.toString()) }
        }
    }
    return answer
}

Java with an executor:

import java.util.concurrent.*;

static final ExecutorService SHADOW = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4); // bounded: protects the app

static String handle(Request req, Pipeline champion, Pipeline challenger, Store store) {
    String answer = champion.run(req);                       // user path
    if (ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextDouble() < 0.10) {
        SHADOW.submit(() -> {
            try {
                store.save(req.id(), answer, challenger.run(req));
            } catch (Exception e) {                           // never propagate
                store.saveError(req.id(), e.toString());
            }
        });
    }
    return answer;
}

Cost and numbers. Shadow at a 10% sample adds 10% to your token bill during the test. If the production bill is 6,000 dollars a day, a 10% shadow costs about 600 dollars a day extra. Use a sample, not 100%, and stop when you have enough data.

Hazards to design around.

  • Side effects. If the pipeline calls tools (send email, create ticket, charge a card), the shadow copy must run with tools stubbed or in read-only mode. This is the most dangerous mistake.
  • Privacy. You are sending real user data to another prompt or even another vendor; apply the same redaction and data processing rules.
  • Rate limits. Shadow traffic consumes the same provider quota; it can cause real 429 errors for live users. Give shadow its own API key or quota where possible.
  • Non-comparability. Two different valid answers are not a regression. Use a judge with a rubric, not string equality.

Real-world use: shadowing (also called traffic mirroring) is a standard technique in service meshes such as Istio and in search and ranking systems; the GenAI twist is that outputs need semantic comparison.

Everyday analogy. A trainee pilot sitting in the simulator while a real flight happens, making every decision the captain makes, but with no control of the plane. Afterwards you compare their choices to the captain's.

Common interview traps.

  • Running the shadow call synchronously in the request path, adding its latency to users.
  • Forgetting tools and side effects in the shadow path.
  • Treating shadow agreement as quality. Agreement with the old version only tells you what changed, not which one is better.

notes.title: Canary deployments
notes.html:
What it is. A canary sends a small percentage of real users' live traffic to the new version, whose answers users do see, while the rest stay on the old version. If metrics stay healthy you increase the percentage step by step; if not, you route everyone back.

Why it exists. Shadow cannot tell you if users like the new answers or whether the new behaviour breaks their workflow (for example more refusals, different tone, longer answers that annoy). Only real exposure reveals that, so you limit the blast radius.

How it works, step by step.

  1. Define the success and guardrail metrics before rollout. Guardrails are things that must not get worse: error rate, p95 latency, cost per request, refusal rate, schema-failure rate, safety-flag rate, thumbs-down rate, escalation to a human.
  2. Assign users to the canary deterministically by hashing a stable id (user id or tenant id), not randomly per request. Otherwise one user sees alternating behaviour inside a conversation and metrics mix.
  3. Start at 1%, then 5%, 25%, 50%, 100%, with a hold time at each step long enough to collect enough samples.
  4. At each step compare canary versus control on the same time window with statistical care.
  5. Automate the abort: if any guardrail trips, the router flips the percentage to 0 without a deploy.
step    traffic   hold    promote if                              abort if
1       1%        1 h     no errors, schema ok >= 99.5%           any safety flag spike
2       5%        4 h     p95 latency <= control + 10%            cost/request > control + 15%
3       25%       24 h    thumbs-up >= control - 1pt              escalation rate +2pt
4       100%      -       -                                       -

Sample size reality. To detect a 2-point drop in thumbs-up rate from 80% to 78% you need about n = 16 * 0.8 * 0.2 / 0.02^2 = 16 * 0.16 / 0.0004 = 6,400 rated responses per arm. If only 3% of answers get a rating and the canary receives 5% of 100,000 daily requests (5,000), you get 150 ratings a day, so the canary would need about 43 days. This is why you lean on proxy metrics that exist on every request (schema validity, latency, refusal, judge score on a sample) and use human feedback only as a slower confirmation.

Sticky routing code. Python:

import hashlib

def bucket(user_id: str, salt: str = "support-prompt-v8") -> int:
    h = hashlib.sha256(f"{salt}:{user_id}".encode()).hexdigest()
    return int(h[:8], 16) % 100          # stable number 0..99 per user and experiment

def pick_version(user_id: str, canary_percent: int) -> str:
    return "v8" if bucket(user_id) < canary_percent else "v7"

print(pick_version("user-42", 5))   # same user always lands in the same arm at a given percent

Kotlin:

import java.security.MessageDigest

fun bucket(userId: String, salt: String = "support-prompt-v8"): Int {
    val d = MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-256").digest("$salt:$userId".toByteArray())
    val n = ((d[0].toInt() and 0xff) shl 24) or ((d[1].toInt() and 0xff) shl 16) or
            ((d[2].toInt() and 0xff) shl 8) or (d[3].toInt() and 0xff)
    return Math.floorMod(n, 100)          // 0..99, stable per user and salt
}

fun pickVersion(userId: String, canaryPercent: Int) =
    if (bucket(userId) < canaryPercent) "v8" else "v7"

Java:

import java.security.MessageDigest;

static int bucket(String userId, String salt) throws Exception {
    byte[] d = MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-256").digest((salt + ":" + userId).getBytes());
    int n = ((d[0] & 0xff) << 24) | ((d[1] & 0xff) << 16) | ((d[2] & 0xff) << 8) | (d[3] & 0xff);
    return Math.floorMod(n, 100);          // 0..99, stable per user and salt
}

static String pickVersion(String userId, int canaryPercent) throws Exception {
    return bucket(userId, "support-prompt-v8") < canaryPercent ? "v8" : "v7";
}

Because the bucket does not depend on the percent, raising 5 to 25 keeps the original 5% in the canary (nobody flips back and forth).

Where the percentage lives. In a feature flag or remote config (LaunchDarkly, Unleash, Firebase Remote Config, a database row), not in a constant. Rollback then takes seconds, with no rebuild. On Android, remember the app can be offline or on an old version; keep the canary decision on the server, because app releases cannot be recalled quickly.

Canary vs A/B test. A canary is a safety mechanism with a goal of "do no harm". An A/B test is an experiment measuring "is B better" and needs pre-planned sample sizes. They share the machinery (sticky bucketing) but not the purpose. See also: 02_L1 section Rollouts and experiments.

Failure patterns.

  • The canary population is not representative (internal users, one region) so metrics look great and the full rollout fails on a different language.
  • Averages hide pain: overall thumbs-up is flat but one tenant's long-document queries got much worse. Slice by tenant, language, intent and input length.
  • Conversation-level stickiness missing: a mid-conversation switch changes persona or format.
  • Slow burn problems (cost creep, longer answers) not visible within a one-hour hold.

Everyday analogy. A canary in a coal mine, or a supermarket testing a new store layout in one branch before changing all branches.

Common interview traps.

  • Random per-request assignment instead of sticky per-user assignment.
  • Having no pre-agreed abort criteria, so the decision becomes an argument at 2 a.m.
  • Confusing shadow and canary: shadow is invisible to users, canary is visible.

notes.title: Multi-layer rollback
notes.html:
What it is. A rollback returns the system to a last known good state. In GenAI there is not one thing to roll back but a stack of layers, and they depend on each other.

Layer              What changes                       Rollback mechanism
1. Application     code, tool definitions, parsers    redeploy previous build
2. Prompt          system prompt, few-shot, templates flip prompt version id (config)
3. Model           provider model id, params          flip model id in config; pinned snapshot
4. Retrieval cfg   chunk size, top-k, reranker        config version
5. Embeddings      embedding model                    keep old vectors; switch read pointer
6. Index           vector DB contents, schema         blue/green index, alias swap
7. Data/knowledge  documents, permissions             snapshots, tombstones, re-ingest

Why it is hard. Each layer can be rolled back at different speeds and with different risks, and they have version dependencies (see the compatibility section). Rolling back only the prompt while keeping the new model may produce a combination nobody tested.

The golden rule: make every layer swappable by configuration, and release them as a bundle. Instead of N independent switches, define a release manifest that names the exact versions of everything. Rollback means "point to the previous manifest".

A manifest in YAML (conceptual; use whatever config system you have):

release: 2026-11-05-r42
  app_build:       backend-1.18.3
  prompt:          support_answer@v8        (git sha a1b2c3)
  model:           claude-sonnet-5-5        (pinned id, verify snapshot name)
  params:          temperature=0.2, max_tokens=800
  retrieval:       chunk=512, overlap=64, top_k=6, reranker=r2
  embedding_model: embed-v3 (dim 1024)
  index:           kb_v3_embedv3   (alias "kb_live" -> this)
previous: 2026-10-29-r41

Python: a router reading the manifest, with instant rollback by changing the active release pointer:

import json

class Releases:
    def __init__(self, path="releases.json"):
        self.data = json.load(open(path, encoding="utf8"))

    @property
    def active(self) -> dict:
        return self.data["releases"][self.data["active"]]

    def rollback(self):
        prev = self.active["previous"]
        self.data["active"] = prev            # persist this to your config store in real code
        return prev

def answer(rel: dict, question: str, llm, retriever, prompts):
    docs = retriever.search(question, index=rel["index"], k=rel["top_k"])
    prompt = prompts.render(rel["prompt"], question=question, docs=docs)
    return llm(model=rel["model"], prompt=prompt, **rel["params"])

Kotlin:

data class Release(
    val id: String, val prompt: String, val model: String,
    val index: String, val topK: Int, val previous: String?
)

class ReleaseStore(private val all: Map<String, Release>, @Volatile private var activeId: String) {
    val active: Release get() = all.getValue(activeId)
    fun rollback(): String {
        activeId = active.previous ?: error("no previous release")
        return activeId   // in production, write the pointer to a shared config store
    }
}

Java:

record Release(String id, String prompt, String model, String index, int topK, String previous) {}

class ReleaseStore {
    private final java.util.Map<String, Release> all;
    private volatile String activeId;

    ReleaseStore(java.util.Map<String, Release> all, String activeId) {
        this.all = all; this.activeId = activeId;
    }
    Release active() { return all.get(activeId); }
    String rollback() {
        String prev = active().previous();
        if (prev == null) throw new IllegalStateException("no previous release");
        activeId = prev;   // in production, write the pointer to a shared config store
        return prev;
    }
}

Rollback speed by layer (typical, not guaranteed):

  • Prompt or model id via config: seconds to a minute.
  • Application build: minutes (container redeploy).
  • Index alias swap: seconds, if the old index still exists.
  • Embedding model: only fast if you kept the old vectors (next section).
  • Fine-tuned model weights: fast if the previous deployment endpoint is still up.

What cannot be rolled back. Outputs already shown to users, emails already sent, tickets already created by an agent, and data written by tools. Plan compensating actions (a correction message, undo endpoint) and keep an audit trail with the release id attached to every request, so you can find affected users.

Practices that make rollback real.

  • Log the release id and prompt version on every request and trace.
  • Keep the previous release warm (index kept, capacity reserved) for at least one full traffic cycle (a week for weekly patterns).
  • Rehearse the rollback in staging. An untested rollback is a hope.
  • Automate abort-and-rollback on guardrail triggers, with a human notification.
  • Treat the provider as a layer: have a fallback model id configured for "provider deprecates or degrades model".

Real-world flavour: feature-flag platforms and model registries (MLflow, SageMaker, Vertex AI) provide the pointer-swap pattern; vector databases such as Qdrant and Elasticsearch/OpenSearch offer collection or index aliases for atomic swaps (check each product's docs for exact commands).

Everyday analogy. A music mixing desk where every slider has a saved scene. Rolling back means loading the previous scene, not nudging eight sliders by memory.

Common interview traps.

  • Rolling back one layer and ignoring the dependency on others (old prompt with a new model, or old embeddings with a new index schema).
  • Deleting the old index or old vectors right after cutover, so rollback is impossible.
  • Claiming "we can roll back" when the agent already took irreversible actions.

notes.title: Rolling back embeddings and indexes
notes.html:
This is the layer people get wrong, so it gets its own section.

Why embeddings are special. An embedding is a list of numbers (a vector) representing the meaning of a piece of text, produced by an embedding model. Searching compares the query's vector with stored vectors. The crucial rule: vectors from different embedding models are not comparable. They may have different dimensions (for example 1024 versus 1536), and even if the dimension matches, the coordinate systems are unrelated. Mixing them gives meaningless similarity scores with no error message.

So changing the embedding model means re-embedding the whole corpus into a new index. This is a migration, and it must be reversible.

Blue/green index migration, step by step.

  1. Create a new index kb_v4 (green) beside the live kb_v3 (blue). Never mutate blue.
  2. Re-embed all documents with the new model and write them to green. Record the embedding model id and dimension in the index metadata.
  3. Dual-write new or changed documents to both indexes while the backfill runs, so green does not go stale.
  4. Run retrieval evals: for a labelled query set, compare recall@k (the fraction of queries where a correct document appears in the top k results) and end-to-end answer quality.
  5. Shadow, then canary: route a share of queries to green (the query must be embedded with the new model for green and the old model for blue; the query embedding follows the index).
  6. Cut over by swapping an alias kb_live from blue to green.
  7. Keep blue read-only and dual-writing for a retention window (for example 7 to 14 days). Roll back by swapping the alias back. Delete blue only after the window.
         query
           |
   +-------+--------+
   |                |
embed(old)       embed(new)
   |                |
 kb_v3 (blue)    kb_v4 (green)         alias kb_live -> kb_v3  ==swap==>  kb_v4
   ^                ^
   +---- dual-write on ingest ----+

Cost arithmetic. Re-embedding 5 million chunks of about 400 tokens: 5,000,000 * 400 = 2 billion tokens. At an illustrative embedding price of 0.10 dollars per million tokens that is 2,000 * 0.10 = 200 dollars (verify the price; some embedding APIs are cheaper, self-hosted ones cost GPU time instead). Storage: 5M vectors * 1024 dims * 4 bytes (float32) = 20.48 GB for the vectors alone, times two for blue and green, plus index overhead (HNSW graph links often add a significant extra, verify for your DB). The double-storage cost during the retention window is a real budget line.

Python: a query path that always pairs the embedding model with its index:

INDEXES = {
    "kb_v3": {"embed_model": "embed-v3", "dim": 1024},
    "kb_v4": {"embed_model": "embed-v4", "dim": 1536},
}

def search(query: str, alias_target: str, embed_fn, db, k=6):
    meta = INDEXES[alias_target]
    qvec = embed_fn(model=meta["embed_model"], text=query)   # must match the index
    assert len(qvec) == meta["dim"], "embedding dimension mismatch"
    return db.search(index=alias_target, vector=qvec, limit=k)

Kotlin:

data class IndexMeta(val embedModel: String, val dim: Int)

val indexes = mapOf(
    "kb_v3" to IndexMeta("embed-v3", 1024),
    "kb_v4" to IndexMeta("embed-v4", 1536),
)

fun search(query: String, index: String, embed: (String, String) -> FloatArray, db: VectorDb, k: Int = 6) =
    indexes.getValue(index).let { meta ->
        val q = embed(meta.embedModel, query)
        require(q.size == meta.dim) { "embedding dimension mismatch" }
        db.search(index, q, k)
    }

Java:

record IndexMeta(String embedModel, int dim) {}

static final java.util.Map<String, IndexMeta> INDEXES = java.util.Map.of(
    "kb_v3", new IndexMeta("embed-v3", 1024),
    "kb_v4", new IndexMeta("embed-v4", 1536));

static java.util.List<Doc> search(String query, String index, Embedder embed, VectorDb db, int k) {
    IndexMeta meta = INDEXES.get(index);
    float[] q = embed.embed(meta.embedModel(), query);
    if (q.length != meta.dim()) throw new IllegalStateException("embedding dimension mismatch");
    return db.search(index, q, k);
}

Other index-level rollback issues.

  • Permissions and deletions: if a document was deleted for legal reasons, rolling back to an older index can resurrect it. Keep a tombstone list applied at query time on top of any index.
  • Chunking changes (size, overlap) are also index changes: they need their own re-index and version number.
  • Partial migrations: a half-filled green index returns worse results. Never route to it before the backfill completes and evals pass.

Everyday analogy. Moving a library to a new cataloguing system: you keep the old card catalogue running until the new one is verified, and you never mix cards from the two systems in one drawer.

Common interview traps.

  • "We can just add new vectors from the new model to the existing index." No, spaces are incompatible.
  • Cutting over and deleting the old index in the same change.
  • Forgetting that the query-time embedding must also switch (and roll back) together with the index.

notes.title: Prompt and model compatibility
notes.html:
What it is. A prompt is written and tuned for a specific model. Change one without the other and behaviour shifts. Compatibility management means recording and enforcing which prompt versions are valid with which model versions (and which tools, schemas and retrieval settings).

Why it exists. Real examples of what shifts when a model changes: how literally it follows instructions, how long its answers are, whether it adds preambles, how it formats JSON, how often it refuses, how it calls tools, and how much of a long context it actually uses. A prompt full of "ALWAYS" and "NEVER" shouting written for an older model can make a newer, more instruction-following model over-apply the rule. Different vendors also differ in system prompt handling and tool call formats.

The dependency graph.

prompt v8  --tuned-for--> model claude-sonnet-5-5
prompt v8  --expects----> tool schema search_kb@2, output schema answer@3
parser     --reads------> output schema answer@3
retrieval  --needs-----> index kb_v3 + embed-v3
judge      --calibrated-> rubric r4 + judge model X

If you change any node, every node it points to or from must be re-validated.

Practical rules.

  1. Pin exact model versions in production (a dated snapshot id when the provider offers one) instead of floating aliases like "latest". Floating aliases change under you, so your CI results stop describing production. Verify the current naming scheme and deprecation policy in the provider's docs, as they change.
  2. Declare compatibility in the prompt's metadata. For example a header in the prompt file or a registry entry listing compatible_models.
  3. Make CI enforce it: the full golden set runs for every (prompt, model) pair you intend to ship, in a matrix. A pair not tested cannot be configured.
  4. Track deprecation dates. Providers publish retirement schedules; put them in a calendar or an automated check, and start migration at least one release cycle early.
  5. Schema versioning for structured outputs: if prompt v9 emits a new JSON field, the parser must accept both v8 and v9 during the rollout, because old and new prompts run at the same time in canary.
  6. Rollback-safe changes: prefer additive changes (new optional field) over breaking ones (rename a field). Use the expand-contract pattern: add the new thing, support both, migrate, then remove the old.

Python: a compatibility gate that refuses an untested combination at startup:

COMPAT = {
    # prompt id -> models it passed CI with
    "support_answer@v7": {"claude-sonnet-5-5"},
    "support_answer@v8": {"claude-sonnet-5-5", "claude-opus-5-5"},
}

def validate_release(prompt_id: str, model: str):
    allowed = COMPAT.get(prompt_id)
    if allowed is None or model not in allowed:
        raise RuntimeError(f"untested combination: {prompt_id} + {model}")

validate_release("support_answer@v8", "claude-opus-5-5")   # ok
# validate_release("support_answer@v7", "claude-opus-5-5") would raise

Kotlin:

val compat: Map<String, Set<String>> = mapOf(
    "support_answer@v7" to setOf("claude-sonnet-5-5"),
    "support_answer@v8" to setOf("claude-sonnet-5-5", "claude-opus-5-5"),
)

fun validateRelease(promptId: String, model: String) {
    val allowed = compat[promptId]
    check(allowed != null && model in allowed) { "untested combination: $promptId + $model" }
}

Java:

static final java.util.Map<String, java.util.Set<String>> COMPAT = java.util.Map.of(
    "support_answer@v7", java.util.Set.of("claude-sonnet-5-5"),
    "support_answer@v8", java.util.Set.of("claude-sonnet-5-5", "claude-opus-5-5"));

static void validateRelease(String promptId, String model) {
    var allowed = COMPAT.get(promptId);
    if (allowed == null || !allowed.contains(model))
        throw new IllegalStateException("untested combination: " + promptId + " + " + model);
}

Model migration playbook (when the provider retires a model, or you want a cheaper or better one):

  1. Add the new model to the CI matrix with the current prompt. Look at the failure list.
  2. Adapt the prompt (often simplify: remove old workarounds). Keep a prompt version per model if they diverge.
  3. Shadow, then canary. Watch cost per request: a new model may be more verbose or tokenise differently, so the same text can use a different number of tokens. Measure, do not assume.
  4. Keep the old model id in the manifest as the rollback target until it is actually retired.

Failure patterns. A hosted model alias was silently re-pointed and extraction accuracy fell without any deploy (found by the nightly drift job, not by users, if you built it). A prompt that worked with one vendor's tool-calling format broke when the team swapped vendors. A parser rejected a harmless new field and caused 500 errors mid-canary.

Everyday analogy. Software dependency pinning. You would not let latest pull a new major version of a library into production unreviewed; the model is the same kind of dependency.

Common interview traps.

  • Using a floating "latest" alias in production.
  • Assuming a cheaper or newer model is a drop-in replacement. Test it, including token usage and refusals.
  • Changing prompt and model in one release, so when quality moves you cannot tell which caused it. Change one variable at a time when you can.

notes.title: Vendor abstraction trade-offs
notes.html:
What it is. A vendor abstraction is a layer in your code that hides which LLM provider you use behind a common interface (for example complete(messages) -> text), so you can switch or mix providers (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, a self-hosted model through Ollama or vLLM) without rewriting the app.

Why people want it. Avoid lock-in, fail over during an outage, use the cheapest model per task, satisfy a customer who requires a specific cloud, and negotiate better pricing.

What it costs. Providers are not identical. A thin common interface can only expose the lowest common denominator, and you lose or awkwardly emulate provider-specific features:

  • Prompt caching controls and pricing (providers differ in how you mark and pay for cached prefixes).
  • Tool/function calling formats, parallel tool calls, forced tool choice.
  • Structured output enforcement (JSON schema modes), citations, extended thinking or reasoning controls.
  • Batch APIs with discounts, file inputs, vision/PDF handling, token counting endpoints.
  • Streaming event formats, error codes, rate-limit headers and retry semantics.
  • Safety filter behaviour and refusal style.
Tight coupling                  Thin interface                  Fat abstraction
app -> vendor SDK everywhere    app -> LlmClient -> adapters    app -> huge framework
+ all features, best perf       + swappable, small surface      + many providers
- lock-in, hard to test         - some features via "extras"    - leaky, lags new features,
                                                                  hard to debug

A pragmatic middle path.

  1. Define a small, owned interface for the 80% case (text in, text out, streaming, basic tool calls, usage numbers).
  2. Implement one adapter per provider, each free to use native features inside.
  3. Add an escape hatch: an extras map passed through to the adapter for provider-specific options (for example cache control hints), clearly marked non-portable.
  4. Keep prompts per provider/model where they differ. Portability of code is easier than portability of behaviour.
  5. Keep eval suites provider-neutral: the same golden set is your proof that a switch is acceptable. That is the real lock-in protection, more than the interface.
  6. Do not abstract what you do not use. If you only use one vendor today, an interface plus a tested second adapter is enough; a plugin system is over-engineering.

Another route is an OpenAI-compatible gateway (many providers and servers such as vLLM, Ollama and gateways like LiteLLM or OpenRouter expose OpenAI-style endpoints; verify current compatibility per provider). It is fast to adopt but is itself a lowest-common-denominator layer, and an extra network hop and failure point.

Python: a small owned interface with two adapters (Anthropic native, and an OpenAI-compatible endpoint such as Ollama):

import os
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Protocol
import anthropic
from openai import OpenAI

@dataclass
class Result:
    text: str
    input_tokens: int
    output_tokens: int

class LlmClient(Protocol):
    def complete(self, system: str, user: str, max_tokens: int = 500, **extras) -> Result: ...

class AnthropicClient:
    def __init__(self, model="claude-sonnet-5-5"):
        self.c, self.model = anthropic.Anthropic(), model
    def complete(self, system, user, max_tokens=500, **extras):
        m = self.c.messages.create(model=self.model, max_tokens=max_tokens, system=system,
                                   messages=[{"role": "user", "content": user}])
        return Result(m.content[0].text, m.usage.input_tokens, m.usage.output_tokens)

class OpenAICompatClient:   # works for OpenAI or a local Ollama at base_url
    def __init__(self, model, base_url=None, api_key=None):
        self.c = OpenAI(base_url=base_url, api_key=api_key or os.getenv("OPENAI_API_KEY", "none"))
        self.model = model
    def complete(self, system, user, max_tokens=500, **extras):
        r = self.c.chat.completions.create(model=self.model, max_tokens=max_tokens,
            messages=[{"role": "system", "content": system}, {"role": "user", "content": user}])
        return Result(r.choices[0].message.content, r.usage.prompt_tokens, r.usage.completion_tokens)

Kotlin (interface plus an adapter over the Anthropic Java SDK; verify builder method names in the SDK docs for your version):

import com.anthropic.client.okhttp.AnthropicOkHttpClient
import com.anthropic.models.messages.MessageCreateParams

data class Result(val text: String, val inputTokens: Long, val outputTokens: Long)

interface LlmClient {
    fun complete(system: String, user: String, maxTokens: Long = 500,
                 extras: Map<String, Any> = emptyMap()): Result
}

class AnthropicAdapter(private val model: String = "claude-sonnet-5-5") : LlmClient {
    private val client = AnthropicOkHttpClient.fromEnv()   // reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY
    override fun complete(system: String, user: String, maxTokens: Long, extras: Map<String, Any>): Result {
        val params = MessageCreateParams.builder()
            .model(model).maxTokens(maxTokens).system(system).addUserMessage(user).build()
        val m = client.messages().create(params)
        val text = m.content().firstOrNull()?.text()?.get()?.text() ?: ""   // verify accessors in SDK docs
        return Result(text, m.usage().inputTokens(), m.usage().outputTokens())
    }
}
// A second adapter (OpenAI-compatible, e.g. Ollama) would implement the same interface with OkHttp or Ktor.

Java:

import com.anthropic.client.AnthropicClient;
import com.anthropic.client.okhttp.AnthropicOkHttpClient;
import com.anthropic.models.messages.MessageCreateParams;

record Result(String text, long inputTokens, long outputTokens) {}

interface LlmClient {
    Result complete(String system, String user, long maxTokens);
}

class AnthropicAdapter implements LlmClient {
    private final AnthropicClient client = AnthropicOkHttpClient.fromEnv();  // ANTHROPIC_API_KEY
    private final String model = "claude-sonnet-5-5";

    public Result complete(String system, String user, long maxTokens) {
        MessageCreateParams params = MessageCreateParams.builder()
            .model(model).maxTokens(maxTokens).system(system).addUserMessage(user).build();
        var m = client.messages().create(params);
        String text = m.content().get(0).asText().text();   // verify accessors in the SDK docs
        return new Result(text, m.usage().inputTokens(), m.usage().outputTokens());
    }
}
// Another adapter would implement LlmClient for an OpenAI-compatible endpoint.

On Android, none of this runs in the app: the app calls your backend, and the abstraction lives server-side, so you can switch vendors without shipping an app update. On-device models (Gemini Nano via ML Kit GenAI, MediaPipe LLM Inference) are a different category with different capabilities and are best treated as a separate, optional route.

Frameworks. LangChain, LangChain4j, Spring AI and LlamaIndex provide ready-made abstractions. They save time but add a dependency that lags behind new provider features and an extra layer when debugging. Many teams use them for orchestration and still call a native SDK for the hot path (verify current feature coverage).

Multi-vendor failover. Fall back to a second provider on timeouts or 5xx, but note that the fallback answers must also pass your evals, and costs and rate limits differ. Test the fallback regularly in a game day; a never-exercised fallback usually fails when needed.

Failure patterns. Abstraction hides prompt-caching, so the bill is 3x what it could be. The fallback model formats JSON differently and the parser breaks only during an outage. The abstraction swallows provider error details, so rate-limit errors look like generic failures.

Everyday analogy. A universal travel plug adapter. It lets you charge a phone anywhere, but it will not run a high-power appliance safely.

Common interview traps.

  • "Use a framework so we are never locked in." Behaviour (prompts, evals) lock-in is bigger than API lock-in.
  • Designing the interface from imagination instead of from what you actually call.
  • Ignoring that fallback providers need their own tested prompts and quotas.

notes.title: Cost forecasting
notes.html:
What it is. Predicting what your LLM spend will be next month, and next year, from usage assumptions, so finance and product are not surprised. Unlike servers (cost per hour), LLM cost is mostly per token, so it scales with how much text goes in and out.

The basic formula.

cost per request = (input_tokens * input_price) + (output_tokens * output_price)
monthly cost     = requests_per_month * average cost per request

Output tokens are typically priced several times higher than input tokens. Prices change; the figures below are illustrative placeholders (verify current prices): 3 dollars per million input tokens, 15 dollars per million output tokens.

Worked example. A support assistant:

  • System prompt 800 tokens + retrieved context 1,000 tokens + user question and history 200 tokens = 2,000 input tokens.
  • Answer 400 output tokens.
  • Input cost: 2,000 / 1,000,000 * 3 = 0.006 dollars. Output cost: 400 / 1,000,000 * 15 = 0.006 dollars. Total 0.012 dollars per request.
  • Volume: 500,000 requests a day = 500,000 * 0.012 = 6,000 dollars a day, about 180,000 dollars a month (30 days).

Levers and their effect (on the same example).

  • Prompt caching: if the 800-token system prompt is cached and cached reads cost a fraction of normal input (verify the discount for your provider), input cost on that portion drops. Suppose cached reads are 10% of the price: 800 tokens cost 800/1e6 * 3 * 0.1 = 0.00024 instead of 0.0024, saving 0.00216 per request, about 18% of the 0.012 total. At 500,000 requests: 1,080 dollars a day saved. (Cache writes may cost extra and the cache has a time limit, so the real saving depends on the hit rate.)
  • Response cache (exact or semantic): if 30% of requests are served from a cache at near-zero model cost, cost becomes 0.7 * 6,000 = 4,200 dollars a day, a saving of 1,800 dollars a day.
  • Model routing: send easy questions to a smaller model. If 60% of traffic goes to a model costing one fifth as much, relative cost = 0.4 * 1 + 0.6 * 0.2 = 0.52 of the original, so 6,000 becomes 3,120 dollars a day.
  • Shorter outputs and fewer retrieved chunks: each retrieved chunk of 250 tokens costs 250/1e6 * 3 = 0.00075 dollars; going from top-6 to top-4 saves 0.0015 per request.
  • Batch APIs (asynchronous, typically discounted, verify) for non-urgent work such as nightly summaries.

Build the forecast as a model, not a guess. Track these inputs per feature:

requests/day (by cohort, growth rate)
avg input tokens, avg output tokens   (measure from logs, p50 AND p95)
multi-step factor: LLM calls per user action (agents may make 5-15)
retry/fallback overhead: +x%
cache hit rate
model mix (% per model)
eval/CI/shadow overhead: +x%
non-LLM: embeddings, vector DB, reranker, GPU if self-hosted

Agents multiply cost. An agent that loops with tool calls re-sends the growing conversation each step. If each step adds 1,000 tokens and there are 8 steps, total input over the run is about 1,000 * (1+2+...+8) = 1,000 * 36 = 36,000 tokens, not 8,000. Cost grows roughly quadratically with steps unless you cache the prefix or summarise history.

Forecast with ranges. Give a low / expected / high scenario using the p50 and p95 token sizes and growth assumptions. Compute from real logs. Python example that takes logged usage and projects a month:

def monthly_cost(requests_per_day, in_tok, out_tok, in_price=3.0, out_price=15.0,
                 cache_hit=0.0, days=30):
    # prices are dollars per million tokens (illustrative; verify)
    per_req = in_tok / 1e6 * in_price + out_tok / 1e6 * out_price
    billable = requests_per_day * (1 - cache_hit)
    return billable * per_req * days

print(monthly_cost(500_000, 2000, 400))                 # 180000.0
print(monthly_cost(500_000, 2000, 400, cache_hit=0.3))  # 126000.0

Kotlin:

fun monthlyCost(
    requestsPerDay: Double, inTok: Double, outTok: Double,
    inPrice: Double = 3.0, outPrice: Double = 15.0,   // dollars per million tokens (verify)
    cacheHit: Double = 0.0, days: Int = 30,
): Double {
    val perReq = inTok / 1e6 * inPrice + outTok / 1e6 * outPrice
    return requestsPerDay * (1 - cacheHit) * perReq * days
}

fun main() {
    println(monthlyCost(500_000.0, 2000.0, 400.0))                 // 180000.0
    println(monthlyCost(500_000.0, 2000.0, 400.0, cacheHit = 0.3)) // 126000.0
}

Java:

static double monthlyCost(double reqPerDay, double inTok, double outTok,
                          double inPrice, double outPrice, double cacheHit, int days) {
    double perReq = inTok / 1e6 * inPrice + outTok / 1e6 * outPrice;   // prices: $/million tokens
    return reqPerDay * (1 - cacheHit) * perReq * days;
}

public static void main(String[] a) {
    System.out.println(monthlyCost(500_000, 2000, 400, 3.0, 15.0, 0.0, 30)); // 180000.0
    System.out.println(monthlyCost(500_000, 2000, 400, 3.0, 15.0, 0.3, 30)); // 126000.0
}

Operationalise it. Tag every request with feature, tenant, prompt version and release id; compute actual cost per tag from the provider's reported token usage; alert when actual deviates from forecast by more than, say, 20%; set per-tenant budgets and hard spend caps; review cost per release in the canary (a prompt change that adds 300 output tokens is a +0.0045 dollar change per request at the example prices: 300/1e6 * 15 = 0.0045, which on 500,000 requests a day is 2,250 dollars a day).

Failure patterns. A prompt edit doubled the context and nobody noticed until the monthly invoice. A retry storm re-sent large prompts. A free tier was abused by scripts. A summarisation feature loops over long documents and costs far more than the average the forecast used (p95 versus mean).

Everyday analogy. A taxi meter instead of a monthly bus pass: the fare depends on distance (tokens) and not on the number of taxis you own, so you forecast by trips and trip length.

Common interview traps.

  • Forecasting from the average token count. The tail (long documents, long histories) dominates cost; use percentiles.
  • Forgetting output tokens are priced higher than input and that reasoning/thinking tokens (where a model supports them) are billed as output (verify for your provider).
  • Ignoring hidden multipliers: retries, agent loops, shadow traffic, CI evals.

notes.title: Capacity forecasting
notes.html:
What it is. Predicting how much throughput you need: requests per second, tokens per minute, concurrent connections, and (if you host models) GPUs. With a hosted API the scarce resource is your rate limit (requests per minute and tokens per minute, per model and account tier), not servers.

Step 1: peak traffic, not average. Using the same example: 500,000 requests/day average = 500,000 / 86,400 = 5.79 requests per second. Traffic is bursty; assume a peak of 4x the average (measure your own ratio from logs): 5.79 * 4 = 23.1 requests per second.

Step 2: tokens per minute (TPM). Each request uses 2,000 + 400 = 2,400 tokens. At peak: 23.1 * 60 = 1,386 requests per minute; 1,386 * 2,400 = 3,326,400, about 3.3 million tokens per minute. Compare with your provider's limits (they differ by tier and model; verify). If your limit is lower, you need a higher tier, multiple accounts or regions, a queue, or model routing.

Step 3: concurrency (Little's law). Concurrent requests in flight = arrival rate * average time in the system. If the average request takes 8 seconds (long generation), concurrency = 23.1 * 8 = 185 concurrent requests. This sizes your connection pools, thread counts, and for streaming, open connections on your gateway. A blocking thread-per-request server with 200 threads is already at its limit; non-blocking IO or coroutines fit better.

Step 4: self-hosted models (if applicable). GPU capacity depends on model size, memory (weights plus the KV cache, the stored attention state for each active token), batching, and the serving engine (vLLM, TGI, TensorRT-LLM). Measure tokens per second per GPU under your actual prompt lengths with a load test; do not trust vendor demo numbers. Provision for peak plus headroom (for example 30%), and consider autoscaling limits: GPUs start slowly (minutes to load weights), so scale up early.

avg 5.79 rps --x4 peak--> 23.1 rps --x2400 tok--> 55,440 tok/s ~ 3.33M tok/min
23.1 rps x 8 s latency = ~185 concurrent streams
compare: provider TPM limit, RPM limit, your gateway connections

Protect the system when capacity runs out.

  • Admission control and queues: reject or queue low-priority work first (batch summaries) and keep interactive traffic.
  • Backoff with jitter on 429 and 5xx responses. A retry without a delay multiplies the load.
  • Priority tiers per tenant, per-tenant quotas so one customer cannot consume the whole limit.
  • Degrade gracefully: switch to a smaller or alternative model, shorten the context, or serve cached answers.
  • Load test with realistic prompts (including shadow/canary overhead and CI runs, which share quotas), and ask the provider for quota increases well before launches (lead times can be days; verify).

Python: Little's law and token-rate calculation as a reusable helper:

def capacity(requests_per_day, peak_factor, tokens_per_req, latency_s):
    avg_rps = requests_per_day / 86_400
    peak_rps = avg_rps * peak_factor
    return {
        "peak_rps": round(peak_rps, 1),
        "tokens_per_min": round(peak_rps * 60 * tokens_per_req),
        "concurrent": round(peak_rps * latency_s),
    }

print(capacity(500_000, 4, 2400, 8))
# {'peak_rps': 23.1, 'tokens_per_min': 3326400, 'concurrent': 185}

Kotlin:

fun capacity(reqPerDay: Double, peakFactor: Double, tokensPerReq: Double, latencyS: Double): Map<String, Long> {
    val peakRps = reqPerDay / 86_400.0 * peakFactor
    return mapOf(
        "tokensPerMin" to Math.round(peakRps * 60 * tokensPerReq),
        "concurrent" to Math.round(peakRps * latencyS),
    )
}

fun main() = println(capacity(500_000.0, 4.0, 2400.0, 8.0))
// {tokensPerMin=3326400, concurrent=185}

Java:

static java.util.Map<String, Long> capacity(double reqPerDay, double peakFactor,
                                            double tokensPerReq, double latencyS) {
    double peakRps = reqPerDay / 86_400.0 * peakFactor;
    return java.util.Map.of(
        "tokensPerMin", Math.round(peakRps * 60 * tokensPerReq),
        "concurrent", Math.round(peakRps * latencyS));
}

public static void main(String[] a) {
    System.out.println(capacity(500_000, 4, 2400, 8));  // tokensPerMin=3326400, concurrent=185 (map order may vary)
}

Failure patterns. Launch day traffic hits the provider's 429 limit, retries without jitter make it worse (a retry storm). A new canary or CI eval job shares the production key and starves live traffic. Autoscaled GPU workers take 5 minutes to load weights, so the spike is over before capacity arrives. Long outputs (hitting max_tokens) inflate latency and concurrency beyond the forecast.

Everyday analogy. Sizing a restaurant for the Saturday dinner rush and not for the Tuesday average: how many tables are occupied at once depends on arrival rate times how long each party sits.

Common interview traps.

  • Using daily average instead of peak, and ignoring token-per-minute limits (you can be under the request limit but over the token limit).
  • Forgetting Little's law: slow generations mean many simultaneous connections even at modest request rates.
  • Sharing one API key across production, canary, shadow and CI.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• GenAI releases change text, models and data, with quiet, semantic failures, so green HTTP metrics prove little. Add quality gates, gradual exposure and quality monitoring.
  • Prompt CI: prompts in git, a versioned golden set, tiered gates (cheap deterministic checks first, then LLM judge), N samples per case and tolerance bands against a cached baseline. Size the set with n = 16 p (1-p) / d^2 and watch the CI bill.
  • Shadow: a sampled, asynchronous copy of live traffic whose output is never shown. It finds real-world failures, cost and latency. Stub side effects, respect privacy and quotas.
  • Canary: sticky hash-based bucketing, steps like 1/5/25/100%, guardrails and abort rules agreed in advance, slice metrics by segment, and use proxy metrics because human feedback is slow.
  • Multi-layer rollback: a release manifest names the exact version of app, prompt, model, retrieval config, embedding model and index; rollback is a pointer swap to the previous manifest. Log the release id on every request. Irreversible actions need compensating steps.
  • Embeddings and indexes are incompatible across models: migrate blue/green with dual-write, evals, canary, alias swap, and keep the old index for a retention window. Query embedding follows the index.
  • Compatibility: pin exact model versions, declare which prompts were tested with which models, test the matrix in CI, use expand-contract for output schemas, change one variable at a time.
  • Vendor abstraction: a small owned interface plus per-provider adapters and an escape hatch; the real portability is your provider-neutral eval suite. Frameworks and gateways trade features for convenience.
  • Cost forecasting: cost = tokens in * input price + tokens out * output price, times volume; model caching, routing, agent loops, retries and shadow/CI overhead; use percentiles and tag spend per feature, tenant and release. Example: 0.012 dollars per request, 500k requests/day, 6,000 dollars a day (illustrative prices, verify).
  • Capacity forecasting: peak rps, tokens per minute against provider limits, concurrency by Little's law (23.1 rps * 8 s = 185), GPU memory and startup time if self-hosted, plus backoff, quotas, priority and graceful degradation.

Common interview traps.

  • Describing each technique in isolation. Strong answers connect them: CI gates the change, shadow and canary expose it gradually, the manifest makes rollback one step, and cost/capacity forecasts are checked against the canary.
  • Quoting prices, limits or model names as facts. State them as assumptions and say you would verify them.
  • Skipping the data-layer story (embeddings, indexes, tombstones) when asked about rollback.
